Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 4:

﴿He exalted himself in the land﴾, i.e., he became arrogant and tyrannical. ﴿And made its people into factions﴾, i.e., divided groups, opposed to one another. Pharaoh made the Copts (al-Qibt) rulers, and made the Children of Israel (Banu Isra'il) servants to them. They are the group whom he oppressed, and God wished to bestow His favor upon them and make them imams, i.e., rulers in the land, the land of Pharaoh and his people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 6–9:

﴿وَهَامَانَ﴾ [And Haman]: he is the vizier of Pharaoh. ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَآ إِلَىٰ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰ﴾ [And We revealed to the mother of Moses]: scholars differ on whether this revelation was by inspiration (ilham), by a dream, or by speech through an angel. The first is the most apparent, given her certainty in what was revealed to her and her compliance with what she was commanded. ﴿فَإِذَا خِفْتِ عَلَيْهِ﴾ [So when you fear for him]: that is, when you fear that Pharaoh will slaughter him, because he used to slaughter the sons of the Children of Israel after the soothsayers informed him that his downfall would come at the hands of a boy from among them. ﴿فَٱلْتَقَطَهُ آلُ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ [Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up]: al-iltiqat (picking up) is finding something by chance without intending it. It is related that Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, saw the chest in the sea, which is the Nile, and ordered that it be brought to her. She opened it and found in it a child, and she loved him, and she said to Pharaoh: "This is a delight of the eye for me and for you." ﴿لِيَكُونَ لَهُمْ عَدُوّاً﴾ [So that he might become an enemy and a grief to them]: the lam here is lam al-'aqibah (the lam of consequence), also called lam al-sayrurah (the lam of outcome). ﴿لاَ تَقْتُلُوهُ﴾ [Do not kill him]: it is related that Pharaoh intended to slaughter him, having suspected that he was from the Children of Israel, so his wife said: "Do not kill him." ﴿وَهُمْ لاَ يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [while they do not perceive]: that is, they do not perceive that their destruction would come at his hands. The subject of the verb is Pharaoh and his people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 10:

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void (of everything), (that is, bewildered, with no reason remaining in her).﴾ It was said: void of patience. It was said: void of everything except concern for Moses. It was said: void of the promise of God, meaning she forgot what had been revealed to her. It was said: void of grief, since he had not drowned, but this is far-fetched given what follows. It was said: void of everything except the remembrance of God. It is also recited as fazaʿan (فزعاً) with the zay, from al-faza' (fear, alarm). ﴿Had she not been steadied, she would have almost revealed him,﴾ meaning she would have made his matter manifest. In a hadith: "The mother of Moses almost said, 'Woe to my son!' and went out crying aloud, her face uncovered." ﴿We bound fast upon her heart,﴾ meaning We granted her patience. ﴿So that she might be among the believers,﴾ meaning among those who affirm the promise that God had made to her.

And his sister said to him, "Follow him up" (﴿قُصِّيهِ﴾), meaning: follow him. Al-qass (القص) means seeking a trace, so his sister went out searching for him secretly. ﴿So she observed him from afar (عَن جُنُبٍ)﴾, meaning she saw him from a distance, and did not come near him, lest they know she was his sister. It was also said that the meaning of ʿan junub is: out of longing for him. It was also said that its meaning is: she looked at him as if she did not want him. ﴿And they did not perceive﴾, meaning they did not realize that she was his sister.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 28, verses 12–14:

﴿And We had forbidden to him the wet-nurses﴾: that is, he was prevented, for God made them repugnant to him. (al-maraadi') is the plural of (murdirah), meaning the woman who nurses; or it is the plural of (murdi') with a fatha on the mim and the dad, which is the place of nursing, meaning the breast. ﴿from before﴾: that is, from the first time. ﴿So she said, "Shall I direct you﴾: the one who said this was his sister, addressing the people of Pharaoh. ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾: when God prevented him from the wet-nurses, his sister said, ﴿"Shall I direct you to a household"﴾, and the verse [continues]. She came with his mother, and he took her breast. Pharaoh said to her, "Who are you to him, that he accepts no breast of any woman except yours?" She said, "I am a woman with good milk." So she took him to her house, her eye was comforted by that, and she knew that God's promise is true in His saying: ﴿"Indeed, We will return him to you"﴾ [al-Qasas: 7]. ﴿And when he reached his maturity﴾: mentioned in Yusuf [22]. ﴿And became established﴾: that is, his intellect became complete, and that is with the age of forty years.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 15:

﴿And he entered the city﴾ meaning Egypt (Misr). It is also said: a village around it, but the first view is more well known. ﴿at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾. It is said: at the time of midday rest (al-qa'ilah), and it is said: between the two evening prayers (al-'ishaayn), and it is said: on a day of festivity. It is also said that he had been estranged from Pharaoh and feared for himself, so he entered secretively and in fear. ﴿He found there two men fighting, one of his own party and the other of his enemy﴾. The one from his own party is from the Children of Israel, and the one from his enemy is from the Copts. ﴿So Moses struck him﴾, i.e., he hit him. The wakz (striking) is a push with the fingertips, and it is said: with the whole palm. ﴿And he killed him﴾, i.e., he caused his death, and he did not intend to kill him, but his blow coincided with his appointed time. Then he regretted and said: ﴿This is of the work of Satan﴾, i.e., the anger that necessitated that was from Satan. Then he acknowledged and sought forgiveness, and Allah forgave him. If it is asked: how did he seek forgiveness for killing when the one killed was a disbeliever? The answer is that he had not been permitted to kill him, and for this reason he will say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, I killed a soul which I had not been commanded to kill."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 17:

﴿He said, "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals."﴾ Ẓahīr means helper (al-muʿīn), and the bāʾ (bāʾ) is causal (sababiyyah). The meaning is: "Because of Your favour upon me, I will not be a supporter of the criminals." Thus it is a covenant (muʿāhadah) which Moses made with his Lord. It has been said that the bāʾ is the bāʾ of oath (bāʾ al-qasam), but this is weak, because the phrase ﴿fa-lan akūna﴾ ("so I will never be") is not suitable as the answer to an oath. It has also been said that the answer to the oath is omitted, its estimated form being: "By the right of Your favour, I will certainly repent, ﴿so I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾." It has also been said that the bāʾ is for adjuration, meaning: "Protect me by the right of Your favour upon me, ﴿so I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾." And this verse is used as evidence for the prohibition of keeping company with oppressive rulers (wulāt al-jawr).

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 28, Verse 18:**

﴿يَتَرَقَّبُ﴾ *(yataraqqabu)*, in both places, means: he senses (يستحس) whether anyone is seeking him. ﴿يَسْتَصْرِخُهُ﴾ *(yastasrikhuhu)* means: he calls on him for help (يستغيث به). Musa met the Israelite who had fought the Copt the previous day, and now he was fighting another man from the Copts. He called on Musa for help, expecting him to support him as he had the day before. This weighed heavily on Musa, and he said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided person.﴾

﴿فَلَمَّآ أَنْ أَرَادَ أَن يَبْطِشَ بِٱلَّذِي هُوَ عَدُوٌّ لَّهُمَا﴾ *(falamma an arada an yabtisha bi-alladhi huwa 'aduwwun lahuma)*: the pronoun in ﴿أَرَادَ﴾ *(arada)* refers to Musa, and the pronoun in ﴿قال﴾ *(qala)* refers to the Israelite. The meaning is: when Musa intended to seize the Copt, who was an enemy to him and to the Israelite, the Israelite thought that he intended to seize him, since he had said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided person.﴾ So the Israelite said to Musa: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾

It is also said that the pronoun in ﴿أراد﴾ refers to the Israelite. The meaning is: when the Israelite intended to seize Musa, having seen him attack the Copt, Musa did not do so, because of his remorse for having killed the other man the day before. So he advised the Israelite, saying: ﴿Do you intend to kill me?﴾ The news of his killing of the other man then spread until it reached Pharaoh.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 20:

﴿And a man came running from the farthest part of the city﴾. It is said: he was the believer from the family of Pharaoh (Mu'min Al Fir'awn), and it is said: someone else. ﴿Running﴾, that is, hastening in his walk, so that he might reach Musa and advise him. ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conferring about you﴾, that is, they are consulting with one another. It is also said: they are urging one another to kill you, as you killed the Copt.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 22:

﴿When he turned his face toward Madyan﴾ That is, he set his face toward the direction of Madyan, which is the city of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. ﴿He said: "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right way."﴾ That is, the middle of the road, meaning the road to Madyan, since he had left fleeing with his life and did not know the way. The distance between Egypt and Madyan is eight days' journey. It is also said that he meant the way of guidance, and this is more apparent. His words indicate that he was a knower of God (ʿārif bi-llāh) before his prophethood.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 28, verses 23–24:**

﴿When he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾: that is, he reached it, and it was a well. ﴿They were watering﴾: that is, watering their livestock. ﴿Two women﴾: it is narrated that their names were Layya and Safuriya; it was also said: Safira and Safra. ﴿Holding back﴾: that is, keeping people away from their flock. It was also said: they were holding back their flock from the water until the people had watered. This is the more evident view, because of their words: ﴿We cannot water until the shepherds have driven off their flocks﴾: that is, it was their custom not to water their flock until after the people, owing to the people's strength and their own weakness, or because they disliked crowding with the people. ﴿Drive off﴾ with a ya' pronounced with a damma and a kasra on the dal is a transitive verb, and its object is omitted; its implied sense is "until the shepherds drive off their flocks." Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read yuṣdira with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the dal, meaning they depart from the water. ﴿And our father is a very old man﴾: that is, he is unable to undertake the watering of his flock himself. This old man, according to the majority view, is Shu'ayb (peace be upon him); it was also said he was his nephew, and it was also said he was a righteous man not related to Shu'ayb by lineage. ﴿So he watered [their flock] for them﴾: that is, his compassion for them moved him, and he watered their flock. It is narrated that there was a rock over the mouth of the well which only thirty men could lift; he lifted it alone. ﴿Then he withdrew to the shade﴾: that is, he sat in the shade; it is narrated that it was the shade of an acacia tree. ﴿My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾: he asked God for something to eat, for hunger had grown severe upon him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 25:

﴿فَجَآءَتْهُ إِحْدَاهُمَا﴾ Before this there is an omitted speech, its implied meaning being: "So the two of them went back to their father quickly, and their custom had been to be slow in watering (the flocks). They informed him of what had happened, the man watering them for them. So he ordered one of them to call him to him, and she came to him." It is disputed whether the one who came to him was the younger or the elder. ﴿عَلَى ٱسْتِحْيَآءٍ﴾ It is narrated that she covered her face with the sleeve of her shift (dir'). The prepositional phrase (majrur) is connected to what precedes it, and it was said that it is connected to what follows it, but that is weak. ﴿وَقَصَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلْقَصَصَ﴾ That is, he related to him his story. ﴿لاَ تَخَفْ﴾ That is, "You have been saved from Pharaoh and his people."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 26:

﴿Hire him﴾, i.e., make him a hired worker for you. ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy one.﴾ This statement is a comprehensive and eloquent wisdom. It is narrated that her father said to her, "How did you come to know his strength and trustworthiness?" She said, "As for his strength, it is in his lifting the stone from the mouth of the well; and as for his trustworthiness, it is that he did not look at me."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 27–29:

﴿He said, "I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ — his wife who had called him. Scholars differed over whether he married him the elder or the younger. The name of the one he married was Safur, and it is said: Safuriya. From the wording of Shu'ayb, it is good to say in marriage contracts, "He married her to him" (anknahu iyyaha), more than "He married her to him" in the form (ankahaha iyyahu). ﴿on condition that you serve me for eight years﴾ — that is, I marry you my daughter on condition that you serve me for eight years. Makki said: in this verse there are distinctive features of marriage: among them, he did not specify the wife, nor did he fix the beginning of the term, and he made the dowry a hire (ijara). I say: as for specifying her, it may be that it took place at the marriage contract after this negotiation; al-Zamakhshari has said that his speech with him did not amount to a marriage contract, but was only a promise. As for mentioning the beginning of the term, the apparent meaning is that it is from the time of the contract. As for marriage by hire, it is evident from the verse, and our law has affirmed it according to what is reported in the sound hadith, from his saying ﷺ to the man: "I have married her to you for what you have of the Qur'an" — that is, on condition that you teach her what you have of the Qur'an. Al-Shafi'i, Ibn Hanbal and Abu Hanifa permitted marriage by hire, on the basis of the verse and the hadith, while Malik prohibited it. ﴿And if you complete ten, it is from you﴾ — he made the eight years a condition and left the two extra years to Musa's generosity, so he fulfilled the ten for him. It is said: and ten plus another ten after them; but this is weak, due to His saying: ﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾ — that is, the term mentioned, ﴿and set out with his family﴾ — "family" here means the wife; he walked with her toward Egypt. ﴿a burning brand﴾ — that is, a piece; the jim may be pronounced with a kasra or a damma. Anas is mentioned, and "al-Tur," and "you may warm yourselves."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 27–29:

﴿He said, "I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ — his wife who had called him. Scholars differed over whether he married him the elder or the younger. The name of the one he married was Safur, and it is said: Safuriya. The Qur'an, Surah 28 (al-Qasas), verse 44:

﴿And you were not on the western side when We conveyed to Musa the command; nor were you among the witnesses.﴾

This is an address to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and its purpose is to establish proof (ijjah) for his report of the circumstances of Musa, although he had not been present for them. Al-Gharbi (the western side) is the place to the west of Mount Tur, and it is the place where God spoke to Musa. The decreed command conveyed to Musa is prophethood. As for "among the witnesses," its meaning is "among those present there."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 45:

﴿But We produced generations, and the term grew long for them.﴾ The meaning: you, O Muhammad, were not present to witness these unseen matters which you are informing about, but they came to you through Our revelation. It was incumbent upon the people to hasten to believe in you. However, the matter stretched out over the generations that We had brought into being, so their intellects became dulled and their ignorance became entrenched, and so they disbelieved in you. It is also said: the meaning is, "But We produced generations after the time of Musa, and the term grew long for them, and the interval (fatra) lengthened, so We sent you during a gap between messengers." ﴿Thawiyan﴾ means "dwelling" (muqim).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 46:

﴿When We called⁠﴾ means the speaking to Musa (Moses). The purpose of this is to establish the proof upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), by informing him of these matters even though he was not present at that time. ﴿But as a mercy⁠﴾ is in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi), and the sense is: "But We sent you as a mercy from Us to you and as a mercy to creation through you."

This is Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verses 47–48:

﴿And if not that a disaster should afflict them for what their hands have put forward﴾ — "lawla" here is a particle of negation (imtina'), and the second "lawla" is one of urging (ta'arud wa tahdid). The meaning is: had it not been that a disaster would afflict them because of their disbelief, We would not have sent messengers. We sent them only as a matter of giving an excuse and establishing proof against them, lest they say: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs and be among the believers?﴾ ﴿So when the truth came to them﴾, meaning the Qur'an and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿they said: Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ They mean the revelation of the Book to him from heaven all at once, and the turning of the staff into a serpent, the splitting of the sea, and the like. ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?﴾ This is a refutation of them in what they asked for; the meaning is that they disbelieved in what was given to Moses, so if We had given Muhammad the like of that, they would have disbelieved in it too. ﴿Before﴾ (min qabl) relates on this view to ﴿was given to Moses﴾, and it may relate to ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ if the verse is about the Children of Israel, but the first is better. ﴿They said: Two sorceries supporting each other﴾, meaning Moses and Aaron, or Moses and Muhammad (ﷺ). The pronoun in ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ and in ﴿they said﴾ refers to the Quraysh disbelievers. It has been said that it refers to their forefathers, and it has been said that it refers to the Jews. The first is more apparent and more sound, because they are the ones addressed in the refutation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verses 49–50:

﴿Then bring a book from Allah which is better guidance than these two, that I may follow it, if you should be truthful.﴾ This is a command given in the manner of challenge (ta'jiz) to them. ﴿Better guidance than these two﴾: the pronoun refers to the Book of Musa and the Book of our master Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And if they do not respond to you﴾: He knew that they would never respond by bringing a book better than these two, but He mentioned it with the particle "in" (if) for emphasis in establishing the proof against them, like His saying: ﴿And if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]. ﴿Then know that they only follow their desires﴾: the meaning is, if they do not bring a book, then know that their disbelief is out of obstinacy and the following of their desires, not on the basis of any proof or evidence.

﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it﴾. It means: those Jews who embraced Islam. It is also said: al-Najashi (the Negus) and his people. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 54:

﴿Those are given their reward twice﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three people are given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who then believed in Muhammad (ﷺ); a slave who fulfilled the right of Allah and the right of his masters; and a man who had a slave-girl, freed her, and then married her."

﴿Because they were patient﴾ meaning: their patience in the face of the harm their people inflicted upon them when they embraced Islam, or other kinds of patience. ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾ meaning: they push it away. It is possible that by "evil" is meant the abusive speech that is directed at them, and by "good" the good words with which they reply; or it may mean the evil of their deeds and the good of their deeds, as in His saying: ﴿Surely good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hud: 114].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 55:

﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾, meaning worthless speech. ﴿They say: "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds."﴾ This is said by way of disavowal and distancing from those who utter idle talk. ﴿Peace be upon you.﴾ Its meaning here is disengagement and parting ways, not a greeting; or it is as if it were the peace of withdrawal and separation. ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾, meaning we do not seek them out for dispute and argument in speech.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ It was revealed concerning Abu Talib, when the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him to say at his death: "There is no god but Allah." He said: "Were it not that Quraysh would reproach me for it, I would have delighted your eye by it," and he died upon disbelief. The wording of the verse, however, is general in its application. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ is a general expression. It has also been said that he (the verse) intended al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 57:

﴿And they say, "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land."﴾ Those who said this were the Quraysh. It is related that the one among them who said it was al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Nawfal. Al-huda (guidance) is Islam, and its meaning is "the guidance according to your claim." It was also said that they said: "We know that what you say is true, but if we follow you, the Arabs will snatch us away," meaning: they will destroy us by fighting us for opposing their religion.

﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ This is a refutation of their excuse that people would snatch them away. The meaning is that the Arabs do not attack the Sacred Precinct (haram) with fighting, and God does not allow anyone to destroy its people. The Arabs used to raid one another, while the people of the Haram were safe from that.

﴿To which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾: that is, provisions are brought to it, although it is a valley without crops.

﴿They exulted in their livelihood﴾. The meaning of "exulted" (batirat) is that they transgressed and behaved foolishly. "Their livelihood" (maʿīshatahā) is in the accusative (naṣb) as a specification (tafsīr), as in the phrase "he made a fool of himself" (safiha nafsahu). Alternatively, it is accusative because the preposition has been dropped, so the sense is "they exulted in their livelihood." Or the verb batirat implies a further meaning: "they disbelieved." ﴿Except for a little﴾: this means a little of dwelling, or a little of those who dwelt there. That is, after its destruction, no one lived in it except for passing through on the road for an hour.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He raises up in their mother [city] a messenger﴾

Umm al-Qura (the "Mother of Cities") is Mecca, because it is the first place God created on earth, and because the House of God (al-Bayt) is in it. The meaning is that God established proof against the people of the cities by sending our master Muhammad (ﷺ) to Umm al-Qura. If they disbelieve, He destroys them for their wrongdoing after the clarification has been made to them and the proof established against them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verses 60–61:

﴿And whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment﴾, etc.: a belittling of the world, an encouragement to detachment from it, and an exhortation toward the Hereafter. ﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and who will meet it, like one We have given the enjoyment of the worldly life and then, on the Day of Resurrection, will be among those brought forward [for punishment]?﴾, etc.: a clarification of the disparity between this world and the Hereafter that was mentioned before it. The intended meaning of "one to whom We have made a promise" is the believers, and of "one whom We have given enjoyment" is the disbelievers. It was also said: it refers to our master Muhammad (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl; and it was said: Hamzah and Abu Jahl. The generality [of meaning] is better in wording (lafz) and in meaning (ma'na). "Among those brought forward" means among those brought forward into punishment.

"Among those brought forward" means among those brought forward into punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 62:

﴿And on the Day He calls to them﴾: The verb governing the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is implied, and the subject of "yunadi" (calls) is God Most High. It is possible that His calling is through an intermediary or without one. The object is the polytheists. ﴿"Where are My partners?"﴾: This is a rebuke to the polytheists, attributing them to Himself according to their claim. For this reason He says: ﴿"those whom you used to claim"﴾, so the object is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "you used to claim that they are partners to Me," or "you used to claim that they are intercessors for you."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verses 63–64:

﴿Those about whom the Word has been justified will say: "Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray just as we ourselves were led astray. We disavow before You; it was not us they were worshipping."﴾ The meaning of ﴿the Word has been justified against them﴾: the punishment became binding upon them. What is meant by this is the leaders of the polytheists and their elders. The reference in their words ﴿these are the ones whom we led astray﴾ is to their followers among the weak. If it is asked: how can their saying ﴿we led them astray﴾ be reconciled with their saying ﴿we disavow before You﴾, since they acknowledged leading them astray and yet disowned them? The answer is that their leading them astray was their commanding them to associate partners with God. The meaning is: we compelled them to shirk just as we compelled ourselves to it, but they were not worshipping us; they were worshipping other than us, such as idols and others. Hence we disavow before You their worship of us. Thus what results from the speech of these leaders is that they acknowledged that they led the weak astray, and disowned being their deities; so there is no contradiction in the speech. It has been said regarding the meaning of the verse other than this, but it is a far-fetched strained interpretation. ﴿If only they had been guided﴾: there are four interpretations of it. The first: the meaning is, if only they had been guided in the world, they would not have worshipped idols. The second: if only they had been guided, they would not have been punished. The third: if only they had been guided in the Hereafter, by some stratagem through which they could ward off the punishment, they would have done it. Thus "law" (lau) in these statements is a particle of impossibility (imtina') and its answer is omitted. The fourth: that it is for wishing, i.e., they wished that they had been guided.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 68:

﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses.﴾ It has been said: its occasion was the astonishment of the Quraysh at the exclusive election of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) to prophethood. So the meaning is that Allah creates whatever He wills, and chooses for His message whomever He wills of His servants. Its wording is more general than that, and it is better to take it in its generality: that is, He chooses whatever He wills among affairs absolutely, and does whatever He intends. ﴿They have no choice.﴾ Here "mā" is negative, and the meaning is: the servants have no choice; choice and will belong to Allah alone. So the pause is on His saying "wa yakhtār" (and He chooses). It has also been said that "mā" is the object of "yakhtār," and the meaning of "khiyarah" (choice) on this reading is good and benefit (maṣlaḥah). This follows the view of the Mu'tazilah, and it is weak, because "al-khiyarah" is in the nominative as the subject of "kāna" (was). Had "mā" been the object, the subject of "kāna" would have been a pronoun referring back to "mā," and "al-khiyarah" would have been in the accusative as the predicate of "kāna." Whoever said that "mā" is the object has offered an excuse for this by saying: the sense of the sentence is "He chooses what they had choice in," then the prepositional phrase was deleted; but this is weak. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: it is plausible that "mā" be the object if we take "kāna" as complete (tāmmah), and one pauses at His saying "mā kān" (what was): that is, He chooses every existent thing; and "lahum al-khiyarah" (they have the choice) would be a new independent sentence. But this is very far-fetched.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 69:

﴿He knows what their breasts conceal﴾. That is, what their hearts hide. He expressed the heart by the breast, because the breast contains it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verses 70–73:

﴿To Him belongs praise in the first life and the Hereafter﴾. It is said that the praise in the Hereafter is their saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ [al-Zumar: 74], or their saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾ [Fatir: 34]. In mentioning the first life together with the Hereafter there is a correspondence (mutabaqah). ﴿Perpetual﴾ (sarmadan), meaning continuous. The purpose of the verses is to establish the oneness of God and to nullify association with Him (shirk). If it is asked: how did He say ﴿would bring you light﴾ (bi-diya'), and why did He not say "would bring you day," in contrast to His saying ﴿would bring you night﴾? The answer is that He mentioned "light" for the sake of all the benefits and lessons contained in it. ﴿So that you may rest therein﴾, meaning in the night, ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾, meaning in the day. In the verse there is thus a figure of speech called laff wa nashr (the arrangement of two things followed by their corresponding parts in order).

And We will draw out from every nation a witness ﴿and We will draw out from every nation a witness﴾, meaning: We will bring forth from every nation a witness from among them who testifies against them concerning their deeds, and he is their prophet, because every prophet bears witness over his nation. ﴿Say: "Bring your proof!"﴾, meaning: bring your argument for what you were upon of disbelief. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 76:

﴿Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Musa﴾: that is, from the Children of Israel. He was a cousin of Musa; it is also said he was his paternal cousin, and it is also said he was his maternal cousin. ﴿So he transgressed against them﴾: that is, he became arrogant and tyrannical. Among that was his disbelief in Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿And We gave him of the treasures what its keys would indeed weigh down a group of strong men with﴾: The "mafatih" (keys) are those with which something is opened. It is also said that they are the storehouses, but the first meaning is more apparent. The "usbah" (group) is a company of men from ten to forty. "Tanu'" means to weigh down; it is said "naa bihi al-hamlu" when the load has burdened him. It is also said that the meaning of "tanu'" is to rise up with strain and effort. The appropriate reading according to this view is that the group would be the ones who strain under the keys, but the expression has been inverted, as inversion of speech is frequently found in the Arabic usage; on the first view, no inversion is needed. ﴿Do not exult﴾: The exultation here is that which leads to self-admiration and tyranny, and therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love those who exult﴾. It is also said that it refers to joy in worldly things, because only one who is heedless of the Hereafter rejoices in them, and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿And do not exult over what He has given you﴾ [al-Hadid: 23].

﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter﴾: i.e., intend the Hereafter with the wealth Allah has bestowed upon you, by doing good deeds and giving charity. ﴿And do not forget your share of this world﴾: i.e., do not neglect your portion of your worldly life, and enjoy it along with your work, since your work in it is only of value insofar as it involves good. On this reading, the statement is an exhortation. On the first reading, it is a permission to enjoy the world, so that he would not recoil from accepting admonition. ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾: i.e., do good to the servants of Allah as Allah has done good to you by granting you wealth. He said: ﴿I have only been given it on account of knowledge I possess﴾. When his people admonished him, he answered them with this, as a rejection of them and a turning away from the admonition they had imposed on him. The meaning is: this wealth was given to me by Allah because I deserved it, on account of a knowledge I possess through which I merited it. Scholars differed about this knowledge. It was said: it is the knowledge of al-Kimiya' (alchemy). It was said: it is experience in affairs and knowledge of ways of earning. It was said: it is his memorization of the Tawrat (Torah), but this is far-fetched, since he was a disbeliever. It was said: the meaning is that I was given it upon knowledge from Allah and a special distinction He bestowed upon me; then he made his words "with me" like your saying "in my opinion and belief." ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations﴾: this is a refutation of him for being deluded by the world and for his abundant accumulation of wealth, or his accumulation of servants. The first is more apparent.

﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾: regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first is that it is connected to what precedes it, and the pronoun in "their sins" refers to the earlier generations, so that the meaning is: the criminals of later times will not be asked about the sins of those who came before them, the destroyed nations, because each person is asked only about his own sins. The second is that it is information about the state of the criminals in the Hereafter, that they will not be asked about their sins because they will enter the Fire without reckoning. The sound view is that they will be held to account for their sins and will be questioned about them, based on His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr 15:92–93]. The questioning that is negated is questioning in the manner of inquiry and seeking information, since there is no need to question them in that manner; rather, they are questioned in the manner of rebuke. Wherever the Qur'an affirms questioning in the Hereafter, it means reckoning and rebuke, and wherever it negates it, it means inquiry and seeking information. Among this is His saying: ﴿So on that Day, no man or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ [al-Rahman 55:39].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verses 79–82:

﴿So he went out before his people in his finery.﴾ It is said he wore red garments; it is also said he went out with his servants and retinue, though the wording is more general than that. ﴿Woe to you!﴾ A rebuke to those who wished for the like of Qarun's condition. ﴿But none shall receive it except the patient.﴾ The pronoun refers to the qualities indicated by the preceding discourse, namely faith and righteous deeds. It is also said that it refers to the word spoken by those who were given knowledge: that is, the word is only uttered by the patient. Patience here means restraining the self from this world and its adornments. ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home.﴾ It is related that when Qarun oppressed the Children of Israel and harmed Musa, Musa (peace be upon him) invoked against him. Allah revealed to him that He had commanded the earth to obey him regarding Qarun and his followers. Musa said: "O earth, seize them!" So it seized them up to their knees; they cried out to Musa, and he said: "O earth, seize them!" until the sinking was complete with them. ﴿In his place﴾ means in his station in wealth and honour. ﴿Yesterday﴾ may mean the day before that day, or the recent time that had passed. ﴿Wayka'anna﴾: According to Sibawayh's view, "way" is an interjection (harf tanbih, a particle of alerting), after which "ka'anna" (as if) was added; the meaning on this view is that they became alert to their error in saying: ﴿Would that we had the like of what Qarun was given!﴾ Then they said: ﴿Wayka'anna Allah spreads provision for whomever He wills of His servants, and restricts it﴾, meaning: how similar the situation is to this. The Kufans said: "wayk" is "waylak" with the lam dropped due to frequent usage, and then "anna" was added after it; the meaning is: did they not know that Allah...? It is also said that "wayka'anna" is a single word meaning: did you not know?

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 85:

﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an upon you will surely return you to a place of return.﴾ That is, He sent it down to you and established it. It was also said that the meaning is "He gave you the Qur'an," and the meanings are close. It was also said that it means "He imposed upon you the rulings of the Qur'an," and so it is by omission of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), the original being "the rulings of the Qur'an." ﴿Will surely return you to a place of return﴾: al-ma'ad (the place of return) is the place to which one is returned. It was said: it means Makkah, and the verse was revealed at the time of the Hijrah, so it contains a promise of return to Makkah and its conquest. It was also said: it means the Hereafter, so its meaning is an announcement of the gathering (al-ḥashr). And it was said: it means Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 86:

﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you﴾ That is: you did not hope to attain prophethood, nor that the Book would be sent down to you. But Allah showed you mercy by this, and showed mercy to the people through your prophethood. The exception (al-istithna') here carries the sense of "but" (lakin), so it is disjunctive (munqati'). It may also be connected (muttasil). The meaning would then be: the Book was not sent down to you except as a mercy from your Lord to you and a mercy to the people. "Mercy" (rahmah) in this reading is either an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih) or a circumstantial state (hal); on the first reading, it is in the accusative as an exception (mansub 'ala al-istithna').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 28, verse 87–88:

﴿And call (people) to your Lord﴾. It may be that this is from "du'a'" in the sense of supplication and entreaty, or from calling people to faith in God. On this latter reading the object is omitted, its implied sense being: call the people. ﴿And do not call upon﴾, i.e., do not worship, ﴿another god along with God. There is no god but Him. Everything will perish except His Face﴾ (the verse). That is, except Him, and "face" here is an expression for the Essence.
